newsitem.title: INDIA: India government possible by Sunday--United Front.
newsitem.headline: India government possible by Sunday--United Front.

text.p: India's toppled United Front coalition said on Wednesday there was a "distinct possibility" that a new government under its leadership would be forged in the next few days.

A senior coalition official was asked by reporters to comment on the 1997/97 (April-March) budget, set to be taken up by parliament on April 21 but called into question by left-wing parties and the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

"If a government can be formed, which is a distinct possibility, before the 20th, that budget will be handled by the new government," said the official, who asked not to be identified. "That's the hope on which we all are proceeding."
President Shankar Dayal Sharma has called a special session of parliament between April 21 and 23 to allow discussion and a possible vote on the budget.

The Congress party, which triggered the fall of Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's government last week by withdrawing its support, said on Monday that it would support a new United Front government provided the alliance named a new leader.
"There is no question of a coalition with the Congress party at all. The consensus is that there should be no coalition," the United Front official said.

The United Front's decision-making Steering Committee is set to meet on Thursday at 3 p.m. (0930 GMT) to discuss a possible leadership change. Members of parliament from the 15 parties in the alliance were scheduled to endorse a new leader on Sunday.
"The consensus on change of leadership as demanded by Congress has not yet emerged. The Left parties are yet to take a view," the United Front official said.
The four left-wing parties in the United Front, including two communist groups, were to meet in Delhi later on Wednesday.
A southern politician close to the Nehru-Gandhi dynasty emerged as a front-runner to become India's next prime minister.
G.K. Moopanar, who defected from the Congress party last year to form a regional party in Tamil Nadu state, appeared well placed ahead of the United Front Steering Committee meeting.
Moopanar was joined by a long list of hopefuls and was by no means assured of being picked to succeed Deve Gowda.
As a former Congress member, Moopanar is seen as a link between the United Front and Congress. He is close to Sonia Gandhi, the widow of the late prime minister Rajiv Gandhi.

But his detractors in the United Front said Moopanar lacks experience in governance. He also was said to be opposed by the leader of Deve Gowda's Janata Dal party, Laloo Prasad Yadav, himself a candidate for prime minister.
